newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco stocks wait to exhale after bad market day.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco stocks wait to exhale after bad market day.

text.p: Investors in tobacco stocks held their breath on Thursday as industry leaders like Philip Morris Cos Inc plummeted almost ten percent on rekindled litigation worries and an overall weak market.
But analysts say investors should relax and buy at these bargain prices, citing the industry's robust earnings growth, and strong defenses against litigation.
"I see these threats as buying opportunities," said Smith Barney analyst Martin Feldman.
"Buy on the dips and that is how you accumulate and make money on the stocks," he told television channel CNBC.
On the New York Stock Exchange, shares of Philip Morris plunged 10-3/4 to 126 by the close. RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp dropped 2-7/8 to 34-1/4, Loews Corp fell 6 to 104-3/8.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 160 points or 2.25 percent. About 30 points of that fall was due to the decrease in Philip Morris shares.
Two blows landed on Thursday.
The Mississippi Supreme Court on Thursday rejected a legal challenge by Governor Kirk Fordice to his own state attorney general allowing a suit to recover state Medicaid funds to proceed.
Mississippi Attorney General Michael Moore is seeking redress for state Medicaid funds spent treating poor people who suffered smoking related illnesses.
This is the first of 22 such suits filed by state attorney generals across the country seeking to recoup Medicaid costs.
Second, Liggett Group Inc, a unit of Brook Group Ltd, is preparing to expand its negotiated settlement of tobacco liability suits to dozens of those states, sources told Reuters on Wednesday.
Liggett struck its landmark settlement in New Orleans a year ago to settle a federal class-action lawsuit. Any deal which expands the settlement is seen pressuring other tobacco firms to follow suit.
Brook Group shares rose 1/4 to 4-1/2.
Analysts noted that it was a nerve-testing time for shareholders, watching court cases proceeding one by one.
"Over the next five months I would be looking for a little more volatility in the (tobacco stocks)," Feldman said.
But analysts repeated that the rate of earnings growth, the legal defences and already weak share prices should soothe fears.
"The fundamentals of the business are extremely strong, Philip Morris is growing its earnings by about 18 percent (per year) and...its defences are incredible," he said.
No tobacco company has been forced to pay a cent in damages in a U.S. court, and the industry argues that long-standing health warnings on packs are a strong defense against most charges.

PaineWebber's Emanuel Goldman said the threat that Liggett will release industry documents that imply a higher degree of culpability by the industry in personal injuries was toothless, because the documents "are nothing."
"Even with those documents, you have to prove fraud at the highest level (of a tobacco company), and that's the hard part here," Goldman said.
"Today's fall was an $11 gift on Philip Morris," Feldman said.
(( Nick Louth, New York Newsroom 212 859 1712))
